en: The Ritual for the Ceremonies of Rising and Sitting of the Stone Buddha in Wuzhong,
compiled by the Tiantai Mountain monk Youxi Chuan Deng.
All pay homage with reverence.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate to the eternally abiding Triple Gem of the ten directions. (After one prostration, kneel with right knees on the ground, burn incense, and scatter flowers.
May these clouds of incense and flowers pervade the realms of the ten directions;
Throughout the boundless Buddha-lands, may they be adorned with immeasurable fragrances, Fully perfecting the path of the Bodhisattvas, And accomplishing the fragrance of the Tathāgata.

(Pause the chanting and say: "May these incense and flowers of mine pervade the ten directions... [until] ...together enter non-arising and realize Buddha-wisdom. Having finished this visualization, chant:
"Having completed the offerings, all pay homage with reverence" (one prostration, then kneeling alternately, recite the praise).
The Buddha’s face is like the pure, full moon; It is also like a thousand suns emitting radiant light.
His eyes are pure, long, and wide like blue lotuses; His teeth are white, even, and closely set like jade or snow.
The Buddha’s virtues are boundless like the great ocean, With infinite wondrous jewels accumulated within.
The water of wisdom and virtue is ever full; hundreds of thousands of supreme concentrations completely fill [your being].
The marks of the wheels upon your soles are all adorned, with hubs, rims, and a thousand spokes, all perfectly even.
Your hands and feet are universally graced with webbing, fully endowed with the characteristics like those of the king of geese.
The Buddha’s body blazes forth like a mountain of gold, pure, extraordinary, and without peer;
like Mount Sumeru, it is replete with merit. Therefore, I bow my head to the King of Mountains among Buddhas.
His marks and signs are as unfathomable as space, surpassing a thousand suns in the radiance they emit.
All are like flames and illusions, inconceivable; therefore, I bow my head with a mind free from attachment.
(Having finished the praise, he again burned incense and lit lamps, and prostrated before the various marks and signs of excellence.)
The soles of his feet are level and even like the bottom of a casket;
his soles bear the mark of a thousand-spoked wheel;
the fingers and toes of his hands and feet are longer than those of other men.
The hands and feet are soft and supple, surpassing other parts of the body;
the fingers and toes are joined by a webbed membrane, surpassing that of other people;
the heels are complete, full, and beautiful.
The instep is high and well-proportioned to the heels;
with single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the past Buddhas Vipaśyin and Kāśyapa; the hands and feet are full;
the hands and feet are supple.
The lines on the hands are clear and straight;
the lines on the hands are long;
the lines on the hands are unbroken.
The hands and feet are red and white like the color of a lotus;
the ankles do not protrude;
the nails are the color of red copper, thin, fine, and smooth.
The fingers are long, slender, and rounded;
the lines on the fingers are hidden and covered;
and the veins are deep-set and do not appear.
The hands and feet are soft, pure, and smooth;
the hands and feet possess the marks of excellence;
and the calves are as slender and beautiful as those of the king of the eneya deer.
The kneecaps are firm, well-set, and perfectly rounded;
standing upright, his hands reach and touch his knees;
his male organ is concealed within a sheath like that of a horse king.
The navel is deep, round, and beautiful.
With a single mind, I pay homage to the past Buddhas Vipaśyin and Kāśyapa. Their navels do not protrude;
their abdomens do not bulge.
His abdomen is slender;
his bodily orifices are complete;
and his body is equal in length and breadth.
His body is as solid as Nārāyaṇa;
his joints are like interlocking hooks and chains;
his upper body is like that of a lion king.
The body is pure; the body is supple; the body is not crooked.
The body is lustrous;
the body is self-sustained and not crooked;
the body is fully developed.
The body is not swaying;
the body is dignified and steady; the body is vast.
His body is tall; with a single-minded devotion, he pays homage to the past Buddhas Vipaśyin and Kāśyapa; his body is upright and straight;
his shoulders are rounded and well-proportioned.
Each and every pore is blue and soft;
the hairs point upward and curl to the right.
The body hairs are red in color;
the body hairs are soft and pure;
the skin is thin, fine, and smooth, such that it does not retain dust or water (and mosquitoes or gadflies do not alight upon it).
The seven parts of his body are full: the two soles of his feet, the two palms of his hands, the two shoulders, and the back of his neck;
his two armpits are full;
and his pores emit a fragrant scent.
The jaw is like that of a lion;
the color of the lips is like the *bimba* fruit;
he possesses forty teeth in their entirety.
The teeth are white, even, and closely set with deep roots;
the four canine teeth are the whitest and largest;
the four canine teeth are white and sharp.
The tongue is thin, covering the face up to the hairline.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the past Buddhas Vipaśyin and Kāśyapa. The color of the tongue is crimson;
the tongue is thin and broad.
He accords with the voices of sentient beings without increasing or decreasing;
he teaches the Dharma without attachment;
he teaches the Dharma according to the languages of sentient beings.
The voice issues forth sounds that inform the multitude;
He preaches the Dharma with sequential causes and conditions;
The moisture and fluids in his throat obtain the most excellent of flavors.
The mouth emits unsurpassed fragrance;
it is endowed with all vocal qualities;
and its speech and sound reach afar.
His Brahma-voice is deep and far-reaching, like the sound of the kalaviṅka bird;
he speaks with harmony and joy according to the inclinations of sentient beings;
his face is not more than one zhang in length.
With a correct countenance and a complexion free from distortion;
his facial features are complete and his face is broad and beautiful.
With a face as pure and full as the moon,
I single-mindedly prostrate to the past Buddhas Vipaśyin and Kāśyapa; his nose is high with the nostrils concealed,
and the color of his eyes is like refined gold.
Eyelashes like those of a bull king;
eyes wide and long;
gazing upon sentient beings with an even gaze.
He does not disparage sentient beings;
his eyebrows are like the crescent moon, the color of deep blue lapis lazuli;
between his eyebrows is a white tuft of hair like tūla-cotton.
The lobes of the ears are formed with the marks of spokes;
the head is like a *mātuluṅga* fruit;
and the hair is long and beautiful.
The hair is unattractive;
the hair whorls are disordered;
the hair color is like that of a blue gem.
The crown of the head is formed with a fleshly protuberance (uṣṇīṣa),
possessing the mark of the invisible crown;
its golden radiance is subtle and wondrous in appearance.
The radiance from his body and face each extends one zhang;
with single-minded devotion, he prostrates to the past Buddhas Vipaśyin and Kāśyapa; the light on all four sides extends one zhang each;
the light illuminates his body as he walks.
When walking, his feet remain four inches above the ground and the marks of the wheel appear;
his majestic bearing is like that of a lion,
and his advancing and halting are like those of an elephant king.
He moves with the gait of a king of swans;
his body turns all at once like that of a king of elephants;
his deportment is fully perfected.
His physical appearance is perfect;
he dwells in peace, unshakable by any;
his majesty overawes all.
All behold with joy;
with one mind, they pay homage to the past Buddhas Vipaśyin and Kāśyapa; no sentient beings can fully perceive their marks;
beholding them, one never tires.
All sentient beings with evil minds who behold [the Buddha] become harmonious and joyful.
With eighty-four thousand marks and signs of excellence and radiant light—
(having prostrated, burn incense again, and repent while making this vow):
I, [Name], disciple, together with all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, now sincerely repent.
At this present moment of thought, we are fundamentally pure and radiant, endowed with immeasurable marks and signs of excellence and the light of infinite spiritual powers and sovereign mastery.

This is truly due to the wondrous nature of True Suchness (Tathatā), which remains unchanging while following conditions to form this mere six-foot body, thereby casting aside the hundreds of thousands of clear and vast oceans.

Gathering conditions, they waver within; rushing outward, they flee in wild abandon. They give rein to body, speech, and mind, giving rise to greed, anger, and delusion. Through the three acts of the body and four of speech, there is no evil they do not commit;

through the five heinous crimes and the seven obstructions, there is no transgression they do not create. Vertically, they exhaust the nine generations of past and future; horizontally, they pervade the six sense organs.
Thus, they open eighty-four thousand gates of worldly toil and fully possess eighty-four thousand dharmas of affliction.
From the crown of the head to the soles of the feet, where is there a grove of merit? From the exterior to the interior, everything is nothing but a thicket of evil.
The causes of karma are unfailing; the retributions thereof do not vary. By virtue of meager roots of goodness, one may temporarily ascend to the human or celestial realms;

yet by reason of heavy transgressions, one ultimately returns to the evil paths. Failing to value the Buddha-nature, one buries one’s own spirit. Coming and going in vain through delusion, one merely...

To exhaust one’s spirit while living in vain and dying in futility is of no benefit whatsoever. However, because sin has no inherent nature and its essence is fundamentally empty, it does not change as it follows conditions;
thus, by awakening to this fact of following conditions without changing, one realizes the true nature (*dharmatā*).

This realization certainly does not involve gradual stages. To initiate practice and bring it to completion, one must necessarily rely upon the Exalted One. Through the ten practices of Samantabhadra, one performs prostrations and reverence.
Among these, the five gates of the Pure Land, repentance is supreme.

We respectfully hear that the Sugata Vipaśyin and the Tathāgata Kāśyapa have perfected their single nature throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and their three bodies universally cover the ten directions. They manifest extinction yet are not extinguished;
stone images floated here from the South Sea, and they manifest supernormal powers though they are not supernormal powers themselves; the precious bowl drifted here from the Western Heaven.
Therefore, one knows that the nature of the image is itself the Buddha; its measure is equal to empty space, the three bodies are perfectly manifest, and the four virtues are without decrease.
For those who take refuge, merit increases immeasurably; for those who repent, sins are extinguished as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Thus, exhausting my ignorant sincerity, I prostrate toward the two Honored Ones, casting my body to the ground with its five parts touching the earth, joining my two feet in earnest devotion, and realizing that the nature of both the one who performs the prostration and the object of the prostration is [identical].

Vast and penetrating, the resonance and response are inconceivable. Like the thousand jewels of Indra’s net or the myriad apertures of the jade sky, their radiance reflects one another and their waves mutually merge.

Facing the Honored One endowed with the eighty-four thousand marks and signs, one performs eighty-four thousand rites of utmost sincerity, thereby extinguishing eighty-four thousand afflictions and achieving [enlightenment].
Thousandfold Gate. I pray that you will manifest your supernatural powers and secretly bestow your majestic grace, so that my precepts, concentration, and wisdom may be pure and without flaw;

that my hearing, reflection, and cultivation may be diligent and never regressive; that in every thought-moment I do not violate the nature of reality (dharmatā), and that in every particle of dust I behold the light of quiescence.
Thus, with this very body of an ordinary being, I am fit to become a vessel for Bodhi. I vow to save boundless sentient beings.
I vow to deliver innumerable sentient beings; I vow to sever countless afflictions; I vow to study immeasurable Dharma gates;
I vow to attain the unsurpassed Way of the Buddha. May my mind remain undisturbed at the time of death; With right mindfulness, may I be reborn directly in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing.

There, in the presence of Amitābha and meeting the assembly of sages, may I practice the ten stages and enjoy supreme, eternal bliss. Having finished this repentance and making these vows, I single-mindedly take refuge and bow my head.
Ritual Prostration. (Rise and perform one prostration. Burn incense again. Scatter flowers according to the Dharma. Circumambulate.
Homage to the Buddhas of the Ten Directions; Homage to the Dharma of the Ten Directions; Homage to the Sangha of the Ten Directions.
Homage to Vipaśyin Buddha. Homage to Kāśyapa Buddha. Homage to all the Honored Ones (Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas).
(Recite either three times or seven times. Having completed the circumambulation, go before the Buddha and take the Three Refuges.)
I take refuge in the Buddha; may all sentient beings realize the Great Way and give rise to the unsurpassed mind.
I take refuge in the Dharma; may all sentient beings enter deeply into the treasury of the sutras, their wisdom as vast as the ocean.
I take refuge in the Sangha. May all sentient beings govern the great assembly, free from all obstacles.
[End] of the Ritual for Paying Homage to the Stone Buddha of Wucheng. Bowing to the Noble Assembly. (Concluded)
